headline: Mission-driven engineering firm for institutions, emphasizing meritocracy and solving hard problems over diversity.
identity: Palantir has consistently valued mission-driven work, engineering excellence, and meritocratic hiring—naming the best and brightest to solve critical institutional problems. Altruism language remained steady from 2012–2022 (zscore ~0.5), then dipped slightly by 2026. DEI language was nearly absent throughout: explicit demographic mentions appeared only in 2013 (women in tech panels), then vanished entirely. The careers copy has shifted markedly since 2025–2026, moving away from inclusive framing ("you belong here") toward civilizational mission rhetoric ("ensure the future of the West") and performance-elite positioning ("judged by outcomes," "deep thinking matters most").
fit: You might be a good fit if you are intellectually contrarian, results-oriented, and drawn to high-stakes institutional problems—and if you value meritocratic evaluation over belonging initiatives. The language reaches for people who see themselves as serious engineers on a mission, not those seeking explicit diversity or wellbeing-centered culture.

sections.heading: A stable mission, a shifting tone on who belongs
sections.body:
From 2010 onward, Palantir's careers copy anchored itself in mission: "engineers on a mission," "work for the common good," "solve hard problems." This language persisted through 2024 with little variation. Altruism scores held steady around 0.22–0.23 (zscore 0.4–0.6) from 2017–2023, suggesting the company maintained consistent messaging about purpose.

But inclusion language—how the company describes who fits—has contracted sharply. In 2015–2022, inclusion scores ranged 0.35–0.47. By 2025, they collapsed to 0.18 (zscore –2.56), the lowest in the dataset. The 2026 rebound to 0.37 came via new framing: "intellectually diverse and contrarian," "strong convictions and open minds," "whether you have PhD or GED." This is meritocratic language, not belonging language. It says *capability* is diverse, not that the company actively welcomes underrepresented groups.

sections.heading: DEI language: present once, then absent
sections.body:
In 2013, Palantir's careers pages featured explicit demographic outreach: a panel on "Women on Working in Tech," a "Scholarship for Women in Technology," and a "Girl Geek Dinner." These generated 3 explicit_demographic register mentions that year. By 2014, this language vanished entirely. No subsequent year (2015–2026) shows any explicit demographic language in the DEI data.

The company did not adopt aspirational vague inclusion language ("we celebrate diversity") or structural process language ("diverse hiring committees") as alternatives. Instead, it simply stopped mentioning demographic groups. The 2026 copy pivots to performance-elite framing: "You are not evaluated by distant executives — you are judged by outcomes." This is a meritocratic stance, not an inclusive one.

sections.heading: Recent shift toward civilizational mission and away from wellbeing
sections.body:
In 2025–2026, Palantir's language underwent a marked tonal shift. Wellbeing scores dropped to –0.08 (zscore –2.70) in 2025, the lowest in the series. The 2026 copy introduced new language: "We built Palantir to ensure the future of the West, not to tinker at the margins," and "Tech culture has fallen into shallow consumerism, lacking a greater purpose." This is civilizational mission framing—a stance that appeared in the DEI data as early as 2019 but has now become prominent in job listings.

Simultaneously, performance language strengthened (zscore 0.53 in 2026), with emphasis on speed ("optimize for impact, not consensus"), autonomy ("no top-down instruction"), and outcome-based evaluation. The company is no longer emphasizing perks, learning opportunities, or work-life flexibility—themes that dominated 2015–2022 copy. Instead, it is recruiting for conviction, speed, and institutional consequence.
